citations.quote: WAL allows concurrent readers and a writer (readers never block writers, and writers don’t block readers) which is a big concurrency improvement over the rollback journal.

claims.text: In WAL mode, readers can access the database concurrently with a writer because they read the original database file plus WAL frames, whereas in rollback journal mode, writers block readers during write and commit phases.

citations.label: S1
citations.quote: Locking and concurrency control are handled by the pager module. The pager module is responsible for making SQLite "ACID" (Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, and Durable).

claims.text: SQLite's locking and concurrency control are managed by the pager module, which ensures ACID properties and coordinates access between separate threads or processes.

citations.label: S1

citations.label: S3
citations.quote: In classic journal mode, a writer will obtain locks that prevent other writers and sometimes readers; in WAL mode, locks are different to allow concurrent readers during a write.

claims.text: In classic journal mode, a writer obtains locks that prevent other writers and sometimes readers, whereas in WAL mode, locks are structured differently to allow concurrent readers during a write.

citations.label: S3
citations.quote: WAL: better read/write concurrency, requires shared memory (on many OSes) for coordination and produces .wal and .shm files alongside the DB.

claims.text: WAL mode requires shared memory for coordination on many operating systems and produces .wal and .shm files alongside the main database file, unlike the simpler rollback journal approach.

citations.label: S3
citations.quote: SQLite coordinates multi-process/thread access via file locks implemented by the VFS layer. Lock states like SHARED, PENDING, EXCLUSIVE govern who can read or write.

claims.text: SQLite coordinates multi-process and multi-thread access via file locks implemented by the VFS layer, using lock states such as SHARED, PENDING, and EXCLUSIVE to govern read and write permissions.

citations.label: S1
citations.quote: WAL provides more concurrency as readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers. Reading and writing can proceed concurrently.

claims.text: SQLite WAL mode allows readers and writers to operate concurrently, as readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers.

citations.label: S1
citations.quote: Thus a COMMIT can happen without ever writing to the original database, which allows readers to continue operating from the original unaltered database while changes are simultaneously being committed into the WAL.

claims.text: In WAL mode, a writer appends changes to a separate file while readers continue operating from the original unaltered database file.

citations.label: S2
citations.quote: Each reader sees a consistent snapshot from when its transaction began, and the writer is busy adding to the WAL without touching what the readers are looking at.

claims.text: WAL mode ensures that each reader sees a consistent snapshot of the database as it existed at the start of their transaction.

citations.label: S2
citations.quote: WAL doesn't give you concurrent writes. SQLite still serializes them: at any moment, exactly one transaction holds the write lock.

claims.text: SQLite WAL mode serializes write operations, meaning only one transaction can hold the write lock at any given moment.

citations.label: S2
citations.quote: Long-running readers (analytics queries, exports) don't make writers wait.

claims.text: In WAL mode, long-running read operations do not prevent writers from proceeding with their transactions.

citations.label: S3
citations.quote: In WAL Mode, the database can allow readers to keep reading data even when someone is writing to the database.

claims.text: WAL mode allows the database to permit readers to continue reading data while another process is writing to the database.

citations.label: S1
citations.quote: Effect: Can reduce per-transaction overhead from 30ms+ to < 1ms.

claims.text: Enabling WAL mode and setting synchronous to normal can reduce per-transaction overhead from over 30ms to less than 1ms.

citations.label: S1
citations.quote: In WAL mode, readers can continue reading from the database while writing. The only limit is that only a single transaction can write at any point.

claims.text: In WAL mode, readers can continue reading from the database while a writer is active, though only a single transaction can write at any point.

citations.label: S2
citations.quote: Checkpointing changes this because: - Data must eventually be written back into the main database file That introduces: - Random I/O - Synchronization overhead - Additional disk pressure

claims.text: Checkpointing in WAL mode introduces random I/O and synchronization overhead because data must be written back into the main database file.

citations.label: S2
citations.quote: If a reader is still using old WAL frames: - SQLite cannot safely remove those frames Result: - WAL file keeps growing This can lead to: - Huge WAL files - Slower checkpoints

claims.text: Long-running read transactions prevent SQLite from safely removing old WAL frames, which can lead to huge WAL files and slower checkpoints.

citations.label: S3
citations.quote: The result: a writer and any number of readers can be active at the same moment. Each reader sees a consistent snapshot from when its transaction began

claims.text: WAL mode allows a writer and any number of readers to be active simultaneously, with each reader seeing a consistent snapshot.

citations.label: S3
citations.quote: Network filesystems. WAL relies on shared memory (mmap) between processes accessing the database. NFS, SMB, and similar don't support that reliably.

claims.text: WAL mode is not suitable for network filesystems like NFS or SMB because it relies on shared memory support that these systems do not provide reliably.

question: How does SQLite WAL mode affect reader and writer concurrency?
report_draft: In WAL mode, readers and writers can operate concurrently because readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers [c:t2-r1-c1]. This is achieved by having the writer append changes to a separate file while readers continue operating from the original unaltered database file [c:t2-r1-c2]. Unlike rollback journal mode, where writers block readers during write and commit phases, WAL mode structures locks differently to allow concurrent readers during a write [c:t1-r1-c1]. Specifically, in classic journal mode, a writer obtains locks that prevent other writers and sometimes readers, whereas in WAL mode, this restriction is removed for readers [c:t1-r1-c4]. While readers and writers can run simultaneously, SQLite WAL mode serializes write operations, meaning only one transaction can hold the write lock at any given moment [c:t2-r1-c4]. Consequently, a writer and any number of readers can be active simultaneously, with each reader seeing a consistent snapshot of the database as it existed at the start of their transaction [c:t3-r1-c5]. This snapshot isolation ensures that each reader sees a consistent view of the data [c:t2-r1-c3]. Long-running read operations do not prevent writers from proceeding with their transactions [c:t2-r1-c5]. However, long-running read transactions can prevent SQLite from safely removing old WAL frames, which may lead to huge WAL files and slower checkpoints [c:t3-r1-c4]. The coordination of these concurrent accesses is managed by the pager module, which ensures ACID properties and coordinates access between separate threads or processes [c:t1-r1-c2]. This coordination relies on file locks implemented by the VFS layer, using lock states such as SHARED, PENDING, and EXCLUSIVE to govern read and write permissions [c:t1-r1-c6]. WAL mode requires shared memory for coordination on many operating systems and produces .wal and .shm files alongside the main database file [c:t1-r1-c5]. Due to this reliance on shared memory, WAL mode is not suitable for network filesystems like NFS or SMB because these systems do not provide reliable shared memory support [c:t3-r1-c6]. The official SQLite locking documentation describes the locking mechanism for the older rollback-mode transaction mechanism, while locking for the newer write-ahead log (WAL) mode is described in separate documentation [c:t1-r1-c3].
